reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: Most cases are adenocarcinomas and are often silent until advanced, so many are found incidentally during or after cholecystectomy performed for presumed benign gallstone disease
Chronic gallstones, a large stone burden, and long-standing inflammation are the dominant risk factors; a heavily calcified (porcelain) gallbladder and large gallbladder polyps also raise concern
Symptoms when present tend to mimic biliary colic or cholecystitis, or reflect advanced disease with weight loss, jaundice, and a right upper quadrant mass
Because early spread to the liver bed and regional nodes is common, tumour depth of invasion into the gallbladder wall strongly determines the extent of surgery needed
An unexpected malignancy found on histology after a routine cholecystectomy usually requires re-staging and consideration of a more extensive re-resection
Complete surgical resection with adequate margins, often including a wedge of adjacent liver and regional lymphadenectomy, offers the only realistic chance of cure
For unresectable or metastatic disease, systemic chemotherapy with gemcitabine-based platinum regimens is the standard backbone, and biliary drainage is used to palliate obstructive jaundice
Anatomical association with pancreaticobiliary maljunction and geographic clustering point to both anatomical and environmental contributions to risk
reference.pathophysiology: Gallbladder cancer usually arises from the mucosal epithelium, most commonly as adenocarcinoma, through a sequence of chronic inflammation, metaplasia, dysplasia, and invasive carcinoma. Prolonged mechanical and inflammatory irritation from gallstones and chronic cholecystitis is thought to drive this progression. The thin gallbladder wall and its lack of a serosa on the hepatic surface allow early direct extension into the adjacent liver and rapid access to lymphatics and the peritoneum, explaining the tendency for early regional nodal and hepatic spread.
additionalDifferentials: Hepatocellular carcinoma or hepatic metastases involving the gallbladder fossa
Pancreatic head carcinoma causing biliary obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal ultrasound as initial imaging for wall thickening, mass, or suspicious polyp
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI with MRCP to assess local invasion, biliary involvement, and nodal or distant spread
Serum tumour markers such as CA 19-9 and CEA to support diagnosis and monitoring
Histopathological review of the resected gallbladder specimen with attention to depth of wall invasion and margins
Staging cross-sectional imaging and, where indicated, diagnostic laparoscopy to exclude peritoneal disease
redFlags: Painless jaundice or a palpable right upper quadrant mass suggesting advanced disease
Gallbladder wall thickening or a fixed mass on imaging in a patient with weight loss
Incidental carcinoma reported after cholecystectomy, mandating urgent re-staging
Large or growing gallbladder polyp, particularly over one centimetre
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on stage; tumours confined to the mucosa and found incidentally can have a good prognosis after adequate resection, whereas transmural or node-positive and metastatic disease carries a poor outlook with low long-term survival.
pitfalls: Attributing chronic right upper quadrant symptoms solely to benign gallstone disease and missing an underlying tumour
Failing to send or carefully review the gallbladder specimen after routine cholecystectomy
Not offering re-resection when incidental invasive cancer is identified in an otherwise fit patient
Overlooking a suspicious polyp or porcelain gallbladder that warrants prophylactic or definitive surgery
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
management: Base treatment decisions on stage and resectability, and discuss most cases in a hepatobiliary multidisciplinary tumor board before major treatment; consider clinical trial enrollment, especially in advanced disease.

If invasive carcinoma is found incidentally after cholecystectomy for presumed benign disease, re-stage with imaging and pathology review and consider re-resection in a surgically fit patient, since the index operation is rarely adequate oncologic surgery.

Surgery is the only potentially curative option; prefer an open approach over laparoscopic excision when GBC is suspected preoperatively to reduce tumor seeding risk from perforation or bile spillage.

For tumors confined to the mucosa or muscularis with negative margins, cholecystectomy alone (extraserosal cholecystectomy) can be curative; more extensive resection (liver wedge resection, regional lymphadenectomy, bile duct resection, occasionally pancreaticoduodenectomy) is needed once the tumor penetrates the serosa or invades adjacent organs.

Direct extension into the liver, duodenum, or colon alone does not contraindicate surgery, it just guides how extensive resection must be; distant metastases, major portal vein or hepatic artery involvement, or nodal spread beyond the hepatoduodenal ligament are absolute contraindications to resection.
Use diagnostic laparoscopy and thorough staging imaging before major surgery to exclude peritoneal spread and avoid a non-therapeutic laparotomy.

Offer adjuvant systemic therapy, most commonly a fluoropyrimidine-based regimen, after resection given the high relapse risk, recognizing this evidence is extrapolated from biliary tract cancer trials as a group rather than GBC-specific data.

Consider adjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy individually with the multidisciplinary team, particularly for positive margins or suspected residual disease, since supporting evidence is retrospective and heterogeneous.

For unresectable disease confined to the liver bed or locoregional area, consider chemoradiation; use external beam radiotherapy for symptom palliation (e.g. jaundice), sometimes with a fluoropyrimidine-based agent, though durable tumor control is uncommon.

For metastatic or extrahepatic unresectable disease, first-line therapy is a gemcitabine-platinum doublet, the accepted biliary tract cancer backbone; clinical trial enrollment, including genomic-profiling-directed trials, is an appropriate alternative.
For second-line therapy after progression on gemcitabine-platinum, an oxaliplatin-containing regimen (such as a FOLFOX-type combination) can be considered, though no single standard is established.

Consider genomic and HER2 testing in advanced disease to identify candidates for targeted therapy or a clinical trial (FGFR2 and IDH1 inhibitors are better established in cholangiocarcinoma generally; HER2-directed therapy shows early signals in GBC), rather than treating these as settled standard of care.

Start palliative care and goals-of-care discussions early in advanced unresectable disease, focusing on relief of biliary obstruction (endoscopic or percutaneous drainage/stenting), prevention of bowel obstruction, and symptom control; surgical bypass or resection of metastatic/distant nodal disease is not generally justified.

After curative-intent resection, follow up with periodic clinical review, cross-sectional imaging, and tumor markers (CA 19-9 and CEA); in advanced disease on chemotherapy, monitor response with periodic imaging and clinical review, and transition to second-line therapy or best supportive care based on progression and performance status.
